categories.name: Comparison of entities
categories.definition: The panel puts named methods, models or variants side by side so the reader concludes how they relate on a metric.
categories.include_if: The main takeaway is about which entity is better, equal or closer to a reference, rather than how a quantity changes with x.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend or regime when the shape of the curve along x is the point and the identity of the entities is secondary.

categories.name: Ours beats baseline (gap)
categories.definition: One entity, usually the proposed method, is clearly better than one or a few baselines, and the size of the gap is the message.
categories.include_if: There are two to four entities, one is highlighted, and the takeaway is 'X is better than Y by a margin'.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-ranking for a full ordering of many entities, and compare-consistency when the point is that the win repeats across facets or datasets.

categories.name: Ranking / leaderboard
categories.definition: Many entities are ordered on a metric so the reader reads off the order, the top entity and the spread.
categories.include_if: There are five or more entities, or sorted bars or tables, and the reader cares about the full order or the top-k.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when only ours-versus-rest matters, and compare-consistency when the order is shown to repeat across settings.

categories.name: Parity / on par
categories.definition: Two or more entities are shown to perform about the same, often to argue that a cheaper method loses nothing.
categories.include_if: The curves or bars overlap, and the stated claim is 'comparable', 'on par' or 'no significant difference'.
categories.exclude_if: Use robustness-insensitivity when the overlapping entities are settings of one knob rather than competing methods.

categories.name: Advantage holds across settings
categories.definition: The same comparative result, such as ours being best or a fixed ordering, repeats across datasets, models, metrics or difficulty levels.
categories.include_if: The panel is faceted or grouped over settings, and the claim uses 'consistently', 'across all' or 'trends are consistent'.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when there is a single setting, and robustness-sensitivity when settings are levels of a perturbation and the point is how much the metric degrades.

categories.name: Estimate vs ground truth / exact reference
categories.definition: Estimates from each method are plotted against a ground-truth, exact or oracle reference, either directly or as an error ratio, so the reader sees which method is closest.
categories.include_if: There is a truth, exact, oracle or reference-posterior curve, or the y-axis is error or ratio to the truth.
categories.exclude_if: Use theory-prediction-match when the reference is a theoretical prediction or fitted law rather than ground-truth data.

categories.name: Trend along a variable
categories.definition: The panel shows how one quantity changes as a variable such as size, budget, time or difficulty increases.
categories.include_if: The shape along x (direction, slope, plateau) is the takeaway.
categories.exclude_if: Use regime when the point is a specific change point, crossover or optimum rather than the overall direction.

categories.name: Monotone / dose-response
categories.definition: The metric rises or falls steadily with x, for example error growing with difficulty or task complexity.
categories.include_if: The claim is of the form 'more X gives more or less Y', with no special point on the curve.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend-scaling when the axes are log-log or compute/size with a power-law reading, and regime-failure-onset when there is a sharp cliff.

categories.name: Scaling law / cost growth
categories.definition: A metric or cost is plotted against scale (nodes, compute, memory length, dimension), usually on log axes, to show its growth rate.
categories.include_if: The x-axis is a scale variable, log axes or power-law fits are used, and the claim is about the growth rate.
categories.exclude_if: Use regime-crossover when two scaling curves swap order and the swap point is the message.

categories.name: Saturation / diminishing returns
categories.definition: Gains flatten as x grows, so extra budget, attempts or data stop helping.
categories.include_if: A plateau or shrinking increments is the stated point.
categories.exclude_if: Use tradeoff-budget-curve when cost and quality are plotted together to choose an operating point.

categories.name: Training dynamics
categories.definition: Quantities are plotted over training steps or generations to show how a run behaves (stable, converging, co-moving metrics).
categories.include_if: The x-axis is steps, epochs or generations, the point is the behaviour of the run itself, and there is no head-to-head method claim.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when training curves are used mainly to show that ours ends above a baseline.

categories.name: Regimes, thresholds and transitions
categories.definition: The panel locates a special point where behaviour changes qualitatively: a crossover, collapse, sudden emergence or optimum.
categories.include_if: The reader is meant to remember an x-value or condition where something switches.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend when the change is gradual with no distinguished point.

categories.name: Crossover / order flip
categories.definition: Two or more curves swap their ordering at some x, so which option is best depends on the regime.
categories.include_if: The curves intersect and the claim is 'A is better below x*, B above'.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when one curve dominates everywhere.

categories.name: Collapse / cliff / divergence
categories.definition: Performance breaks down sharply beyond a threshold or after some time (blow-up, cliff, collapse).
categories.include_if: There is an abrupt drop or explosion and the claim names a failure.
categories.exclude_if: Use characterize-failure-mode for a static breakdown of failure types with no threshold along x, and robustness-generalization-gap for seen-versus-unseen collapse.

categories.name: Emergence / step transition
categories.definition: A property appears suddenly, as a step, jump or onset layer, instead of growing smoothly.
categories.include_if: There is a staircase or jump and the claim is 'emerges' or 'identifies at step k'.
categories.exclude_if: Use regime-failure-onset when the jump is a degradation.

categories.name: Interior optimum / U-curve
categories.definition: A sweep has a best interior value, such as a U-shaped loss or a peak at r*.
categories.include_if: There is a U or inverted-U and the claim names an optimal setting.
categories.exclude_if: Use robustness-sensitivity when the sweep is shown to justify a hyperparameter range rather than to identify an optimum.

categories.name: Trade-offs and efficiency
categories.definition: The panel relates quality to cost (time, tokens, parameters, bitrate) so the reader judges efficiency.
categories.include_if: Both a cost axis and a quality axis are present, explicitly or by twin panels.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend-scaling when only the cost is plotted against size with no quality dimension.

categories.name: Pareto / frontier position
categories.definition: Methods are placed in a cost-versus-quality plane and ours sits on or beyond the frontier, in the 'good corner'.
categories.include_if: It is a scatter or bubble of methods on two competing axes, and the claim is 'best of both' or 'Pareto-optimal'.
categories.exclude_if: Use tradeoff-budget-curve when a single method is swept over a budget.

categories.name: Quality vs budget curve
categories.definition: Quality is plotted against a swept budget (rate, max length, steps, sparsity), often with a paired cost panel, to show where a method sits.
categories.include_if: The x-axis is a resource knob, and the claim is 'better quality at every budget' or 'flat until a knee'.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend-saturation when no efficiency comparison is intended.

categories.name: Cost / overhead comparison
categories.definition: Bars or lines show that ours uses far less compute or memory than a competitor, with no quality axis.
categories.include_if: Only the cost is shown and the claim is about efficiency.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend-scaling when growth with size is the emphasis.

categories.name: Attribution / mechanism
categories.definition: The panel attributes an outcome to a component, cause or part, by removal, intervention or breakdown.
categories.include_if: The claim is 'component X is responsible for Y' or 'Y splits into parts'.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare when the variants are independent methods rather than pieces of one system.

categories.name: Ablation (remove or swap component)
categories.definition: The full system is compared with variants that lack or replace a component, to show that the component matters.
categories.include_if: Variants are named 'w/o X', 'LOO' or 'fix vs default', or are before/after a processing step.
categories.exclude_if: Use attribute-intervention when there is a matched control and a dose knob.

categories.name: Targeted intervention vs matched control
categories.definition: A specific internal component is amplified or removed, often at graded strength, against random or energy-matched controls to establish causal relevance.
categories.include_if: There are control conditions, an α or γ strength axis, or removal from a mechanistic analysis.
categories.exclude_if: Use attribute-ablation for an architecture or recipe component removed without a matched control.

categories.name: Decomposition into parts
categories.definition: A total (runtime, score, competency profile) is split into components to show which part dominates.
categories.include_if: It shows stacked parts that sum to a whole, or a per-component profile of one total.
categories.exclude_if: Use characterize-failure-mode when the parts are error categories.

categories.name: Robustness and sensitivity
categories.definition: The panel shows how much a result moves under perturbation, hyperparameter change, distribution shift or random seed.
categories.include_if: The x or grouping variable is a nuisance or perturbation and the claim concerns its effect size.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend when the swept variable is the scientific variable of interest.

categories.name: Sensitivity to perturbation or hyperparameter
categories.definition: The metric degrades or changes noticeably as a perturbation or hyperparameter varies.
categories.include_if: It is a sweep, or a reference-versus-perturbed overlay, and the claim is 'degrades', 'depends on' or 'chosen setting'.
categories.exclude_if: Use robustness-insensitivity when the claim is 'unchanged'.

categories.name: Insensitivity / invariance
categories.definition: Results barely change across settings of a knob, so the method or conclusion is robust.
categories.include_if: There are overlapping curves or bars across levels of one factor, with claims like 'remains comparable' or 'tracks the original'.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-parity when the overlapping entities are different methods.

categories.name: Variance / stability across runs
categories.definition: Spread across seeds, checkpoints or test sets is the message (a tight method versus a noisy one, or an error margin).
categories.include_if: It is a strip, violin or replicate overlay, and the claim is about variance or stability.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-superiority-gap when only means matter.

categories.name: Generalization / transfer gap
categories.definition: Performance on seen or source conditions is contrasted with unseen or target conditions, often as a train-by-eval or source-by-target matrix with a strong diagonal.
categories.include_if: There are seen/unseen curves or a diagonal-dominant transfer heatmap.
categories.exclude_if: Use characterize-structure when the heatmap encodes similarity rather than transfer performance.

categories.name: Characterization of data or representations
categories.definition: The panel describes what a dataset, representation or model behaviour looks like, without a method contest.
categories.include_if: The reader learns a property of a population or object (shape, clusters, failure taxonomy, composition).
categories.exclude_if: Use compare when the description exists to rank methods.

categories.name: Distribution shape / shift
categories.definition: It shows a histogram, density or binned distribution of a quantity, or the overlap or shift between groups' distributions.
categories.include_if: The form is a histogram, KDE, violin or binned shares, and the claim is about skew, modes, separation or overlap.
categories.exclude_if: Use characterize-dataset-composition for descriptive benchmark statistics (sizes, shares) meant only to document the dataset.

categories.name: Latent structure / organization
categories.definition: Clusters, blocks, spectra, subspaces or trajectories in a representation reveal an organizing structure.
categories.include_if: It is an embedding, block heatmap, eigen-spectrum, dendrogram or latent trajectory, and the claim is 'separable', 'block structure', 'outliers' or 'shared core'.
categories.exclude_if: Use association-agreement when the structure is explicitly matched against an external reference such as geography.

categories.name: Failure-mode / error taxonomy
categories.definition: It shows which kinds of errors occur and how often, or which conditions models fail on.
categories.include_if: There are error categories, confusion matrices, or condition-wise weakness bars (for example symbolic vs NL, naive vs non-naive).
categories.exclude_if: Use regime-failure-onset when failure depends on a threshold along a continuous x.

categories.name: Dataset / benchmark composition
categories.definition: Descriptive statistics document a new dataset or benchmark: shares, counts, coverage over time, lengths.
categories.include_if: It is a pie, donut, count bar or cumulative-growth plot in a dataset section, with no hypothesis tested.
categories.exclude_if: Use characterize-distribution when the distribution is evidence for a scientific claim.

categories.name: Association between measures
categories.definition: The panel shows that two measured quantities co-vary or agree.
categories.include_if: There are two measured variables, neither of which is a controlled knob.
categories.exclude_if: Use trend when x is manipulated by the experimenter.

categories.name: Correlation
categories.definition: Scatter with a fit, or a correlation matrix, quantifying how strongly two measures move together.
categories.include_if: It shows r or ρ, a fit line, or a correlation heatmap between metrics.
categories.exclude_if: Use association-agreement when one side is a trusted reference that the other should reproduce.

categories.name: Agreement with a reference / metric validity
categories.definition: A learned or automatic quantity is shown to match, or mis-match, a reference such as geography, human judgment or detector labels.
categories.include_if: It shows split-triangle or overlay against a reference, a detector confusion matrix, or a metric-versus-perception check.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-fidelity-to-truth when several estimators compete to match the truth.

categories.name: Theory link
categories.definition: The panel connects empirical behaviour to a formal claim, either by checking a prediction or by illustrating a mechanism on a toy case.
categories.include_if: A theorem, bound, fitted law or constructed example is the anchor.
categories.exclude_if: Use compare-fidelity-to-truth when the reference is data rather than theory.

categories.name: Prediction / bound / fitted-law check
categories.definition: Empirical points are overlaid on a theoretical curve, bound or extrapolated fit, and they agree.
categories.include_if: It shows theory lines with dots, fit-then-extrapolate, a bound above a measurement, or a tail-fit check of an assumption.
categories.exclude_if: Use theory-toy-illustration when there is no quantitative prediction, only a qualitative depiction.

categories.name: Toy mechanism illustration
categories.definition: A constructed low-dimensional example (1-D function, quiver field, anchor embedding, smoothing sweep) makes a property such as continuity, an identifiability symmetry or convergence visible.
categories.include_if: It uses synthetic or toy settings, and the claim is 'shows a jump', 'removes discontinuity' or 'converges to the mean'.
categories.exclude_if: Use exemplify-qualitative-comparison when real-task outputs are being compared.

categories.name: Exemplification
categories.definition: Concrete instances (images, outputs, scenes, schematics) let the reader see the claim rather than measure it.
categories.include_if: There is no quantitative axis, or the axis is incidental to showing examples.
categories.exclude_if: Use theory-toy-illustration when the example is a synthetic function built to prove a point.

categories.name: Qualitative side-by-side comparison
categories.definition: A grid of method-by-example outputs or overlays shows that ours looks better, or that the methods differ.
categories.include_if: There are rows or columns of methods on the same inputs, with arrows, boxes or crops highlighting differences.
categories.exclude_if: Use exemplify-illustration when only one method or the input data is shown.

categories.name: Illustrative example / schematic
categories.definition: Representative inputs, outputs, environment renders, method pipelines or conceptual sketches orient the reader.
categories.include_if: It is a single-method example strip, a conceptual diagram, a case list, or a pipeline overview.
categories.exclude_if: Use exemplify-qualitative-comparison when two or more methods are contrasted.

patterns.pattern: Ours-highlighted metric curves vs baselines over iterations/steps (line, bands)
Faceted small multiples (datasets/models), ours lowest/highest in every facet
Grouped means or bars over jittered per-set points, by strategy/model
Method-by-example qualitative image grid with highlights
Toy 1-D function / quiver / anchor-embedding illustration
Overlaid histograms/KDEs by group showing shift or no shift
Estimate-vs-ground-truth scatter paired with error-ratio-to-truth line
Two-variant crossover curves on log compute/parameter axis (often with fitted asymptotes)
Ablation-variant curves with fitted saturating law (w/o X vs full)
Stacked quality-over-cost budget curves (top quality, bottom cost) vs base
Dataset composition pies, donuts, count bars and cumulative growth
Theory curve with empirical dots, or fit-and-extrapolate
Diagonal or block heatmaps (transfer matrices, attention, sorted components)
Multi-metric or multi-setting radar polygons
Cost-vs-quality scatter or bubble with ours in the good corner
Binned or jittered degradation vs difficulty or complexity (line or grouped bars)
Overlapping paired curves to claim parity (Pass@K, loss)
Log-log runtime/memory vs size lines
Failure taxonomy pie, treemap or 100% stacked bars
t-SNE/UMAP/LDA embedding colored by group (separable vs mixed)
Dose-response of targeted removal vs matched random controls
Dual-axis training curves of two co-moving quantities

unused_or_rare: other:method-overview and other:dataset-composition (ad-hoc 'other' escapes, 3 items, though composition is actually common: ~16 items)
tradeoff/pareto vs budget-curve split is used, but attribute/decomposition is applied to only a handful of items and inconsistently
overlapping_pairs: Identical panels in one figure get different labels (iclr26-0731/f4a,c,d are ranking; f4b,e,f,h-k are gap) with no rule about the number of entities.
'Ours best in every facet' is labeled both ways (icml26-5763/f5 vs f9; neurips26-3817/f7 panels).
Overlaid histograms showing a shift are labeled structure (iclr26-3274/f4d-f) but distribution in the sibling panel (f5); eigenvalue trajectories are labeled both (neurips26-3817/f10).
Overlapping curves are labeled insensitivity whether the overlapping entities are methods (iclr26-4047/f3c) or groups (iclr26-3274/f4a-c).
Toy panels with a quantitative limit (icml26-1148/f1c) and quantitative checks (iclr26-2940/f1) are split with no stated criterion.
Static failure breakdowns are labeled onset (iclr26-3274/f8b, icml26-4959/f4a transfer matrices) even though there is no threshold.
Nearly every two-variant ablation curve carries both labels (iclr26-1322/f5-f8).
Error surfaces over d and τ (icml26-2935/f1) and loss-vs-shape-ratio panels carry both labels without a log-scale or power-law criterion.
missing: estimate-vs-ground-truth / exact-reference fidelity (~20 items forced into compare/gap)
generalization or transfer gap: seen vs unseen, source-by-target matrices (~10 items forced into regime/failure-onset or characterize/structure)
targeted intervention vs matched control / causal dose-response (~11 items forced into ablation)
interior optimum / U-curve (iclr26-4363, forced into regime/crossover)
dataset/benchmark composition as a first-class label instead of 'other:'
qualitative illustration vs qualitative comparison split: exemplify/qualitative lumps method contests with plain examples and schematics
metric validity / agreement with human or reference measure as distinct from correlation
axis_problems: compare/gap is over-assigned: it appears as primary or secondary on roughly 30% of items, including distribution shifts (iclr26-3274/f4d-f), embedding separation (iclr26-1185/f2right) and smoothing curves (icml26-2860/f11right-top), so it often just means 'two things differ'.
trend/dynamics is used to encode form (x = training step) rather than message. All 11 regret facets in iclr26-0731/f4 carry it although their takeaway is purely comparative.
exemplify/qualitative is a chart-form label (image-grid or diagram) masquerading as a message. It co-occurs with compare/ranking or compare/gap on most image grids.

Labels are copied across sibling facets regardless of what each facet shows (iclr26-3769/f5 panels labeled parity, iclr26-0731/f4g labeled parity while the stated claim is superiority). Some secondary labels contradict the stated takeaway.
characterize/failure-mode is sometimes applied to non-failures (jagged derivatives in icml26-2860/f7bottom-right, noisy loss in iclr26-4363/f4).
There is no primary/secondary distinction: two equal-weight labels make counts ambiguous, and most items have a clear primary message plus a form-driven secondary.

notes: The corpus is very clustered by paper: icml26-3678 alone contributes about 45 near-duplicate strategy panels, two of which look duplicated or mislabeled (f1e, f7b), and iclr26-0731/f4 contributes 11. Pattern frequencies should therefore also be reported per figure or per paper, not only per panel. Annotate one required primary message plus an optional secondary 'polarity/scope' modifier (ours-better, parity, holds-across-settings), because consistency and gap are mostly modifiers on a comparison rather than standalone messages. Keep form (line over steps, image grid, radar) on the chart axis only, and drop message labels that merely restate form (trend/dynamics, exemplify/qualitative). Add explicit decision rules for entity count (≤4 entities means gap, ≥5 means ranking) and for reference type (data truth means fidelity, theory means prediction-match, human means agreement). Counts here come from a single best-fit assignment and sum to about 500; borderline items (for example training curves vs baseline, before/after RL bars) could move between compare-superiority-gap and attribute-ablation by a few percent.
